assessment orientation (compared to locomotory) decreases risk-taking through increased anticipation of regret.

(1) assessment orientation is negatively associated with risk-taking and this effect is mediated by anticipated regret; (2) locomotion orientation is positively associated with risk-taking but only in the presence of strong affective arousal and this effect is also mediated by anticipated regret.
assessment mode and locomotion mode affect risk-taking through anticipated regrets.

people chronically in assessment mode (vs locomotion mode) take less risk through greater anticipated regret.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the assessment orientation, through increased anticipated regret, leads to lower risk-taking, and the locomotion orientation, through decreased anticipated regret and emotional arousal, leads to higher risk-taking.
assessment and locomotion modes are different ways to cope with risk.

the assessment mode is associated with increased anticipated regret, which leads to lower risk taking, whereas the locomotion mode is associated with decreased anticipated regret, which is related to higher risk taking.
The main takeaway from our work is that

people who are more likely to be in the "assessment" state (e.g., people with an assessment orientation) tend to take lower risk, because they are prone to anticipate regret more strongly, whereas people who are more inclined to be in the “locomotion” state (e.g. people with locomotion orientation) tend to be more risk-taking, because they anticipate regret less strongly.

people with a chronic assessment orientation tend to avoid risk through increased anticipated regrets and people with a chronic locomotion orientation tend to take more risk through decreased anticipated regrets.
the effect of assessment orientation on risk-taking can be mediated by anticipated regret, whereas the effect of locomotion on risk-taking can only partially be mediated by anticipated-regret.
